course_name_original: METHODS OF TECHNICAL REPRESENTATION AND INTRODUCTION TO CAD (DG0242)
course_name_en: METHODS OF TECHNICAL REPRESENTATION AND INTRODUCTION TO CAD
prerequisites: Basic knowledge of algebra, Euclidean geometry, and physics, particularly mechanics.
Elementary familiarity with computers and basic numerical and graphical tools.
Basic knowledge of technical drawing and descriptive geometry (orthographic projections, sections, axonometric views, dimensioning), as provided by the Technical Representation Methods course.
Basic familiarity with the Windows operating environment.

learning_outcomes.text: Describe the principles of geometric representation methods, technical drawing standards, dimensioning, dimensional and geometrical tolerancing, surface texture, and the main design solutions used in mechanical and industrial systems.

Describe the operating principles, resolution, main applications, and limitations of biomedical imaging technologies based on ionising and non-ionising radiation, as well as the fundamentals of image enhancement, quality assessment, segmentation, and visualisation algorithms.

Interpret an assembly drawing and produce correct technical representations of components using views, sections, dimensions, tolerances, and surface texture indications, with reference to technical standards and component catalogues.
Apply fundamental biomedical image processing and segmentation algorithms and organise a workflow for visualisation and three-dimensional reconstruction from imaging data.

Select and justify representation methods, dimensioning and tolerancing criteria, and design solutions appropriate to the problem; compare imaging technologies and algorithms considering image quality, resolution, intended application, and limitations.

Clearly communicate the geometrical and functional characteristics of components and systems through standardised graphical language and technical terminology, including English terminology, and clearly present the choices made in biomedical image processing.

Independently consult standards, handbooks, catalogues, technical documentation, and scientific literature and update their skills in using methods and tools for technical representation and biomedical imaging.
Students learn the principles of parametric, associative solid modeling (constrained sketching, feature-based modeling, the feature/construction tree) and standards-compliant drawing generation.
Students are able to independently build 3D models of mechanical components and to derive the associated 2D technical drawings.
Students can select the modeling strategy (feature sequence and type) that is most efficient and robust with respect to later design changes.
Students can document a CAD model, justifying the representation choices made.
Students acquire a parametric, associative, feature-based way of working that can be transferred independently across different CAD environments.

syllabus_topics: Industrial standardisation: technical standards and technical regulations; levels of standardisation; specification, simplification or typification, unification, coding, and marking.
Methods for geometric representation and properties of representation schemes; principles of projective geometry; introduction to axonometric projections.
Schematic and complete representation; assembly drawings and part drawings.
Mechanical drawing standards; representation by views, sections, and details.
Quantitative representation: standards for indicating dimensions, dimensioning systems and selection criteria; functional, technological, and inspection dimensioning; preferred number series.
Manufacturing deviations and prescribed tolerances; ISO system for dimensional tolerancing; tolerance series and tolerance chains.
Geometrical and positional tolerances; independence principle; maximum material condition; envelope requirement; tolerance selection criteria.
Surface texture: characteristic parameters, measurement, and specification.
Permanent and detachable joints; threads, thread forms, and characteristic parameters.
Standard components used in machines and industrial systems; bearing classification and mounting; basic concepts of power transmissions and their representation.

Practical activities: representation of complex solids, assemblies, machine components, and industrial subsystems; part drawings; surface roughness measurements and verification of geometrical tolerances.
Introduction to biomedical imaging: fundamental steps, typical applications, limitations, and future perspectives.
Medical image formation technologies.
Ionising-radiation-based methods: X-ray imaging, computed tomography (CT), PET, and SPECT; operating principles, resolution, and typical applications.
Non-ionising methods: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and ultrasound; operating principles, resolution, and typical applications.
Image enhancement algorithms: terminology, point operations, power-law transformation, histograms, histogram equalisation, contrast stretching, filtering, and unsharp masking.
Image quality indices and assessment criteria.
Image segmentation algorithms: edge-based, region-based, and hybrid methods.
Biomedical image visualisation and management.
Applications of biomedical imaging to three-dimensional reconstruction and prosthesis design.
Introduction to CAD systems: brief history, classification of systems (2D, wireframe, surface, solid/parametric), hardware and software architecture.

Parametric solid modeling: constrained 2D sketching (geometric and dimensional constraints), primary features (extrude, revolve, sweep, loft) and machining/detail features (holes, shells, fillets, chamfers, ribs); the feature tree and parametric model editing.
Automatic generation of 2D technical documentation: orthographic views, sections, associative dimensioning, derived from the 3D model, in accordance with UNI-ISO standards.
Hands-on computer-based exercises, applied to case studies of mechanical components.
teaching_methods: Technical representation exercises (drawing preparation, formative reviews, discussions)
Biomedical imaging laboratory activities (image processing, segmentation, 3D model workflow)
Independent student work with instructor discussion
Hands-on practical sessions using CAD software

assessment_methods.method: Hands-on computer-based test (CAD model and 2D documentation)

assessment_rules: Students must obtain at least 18/30 in both the written and oral components of the Technical Representation module. The final grade for this module is calculated as 70% written test + 30% oral examination. For the CAD module, assessment is a single hands-on computer-based test; passing an exemption test (esonero) exempts students from this practical test. For integrated course students, the exam consists of a single test with written, practical, and oral parts taken in the same session; if the practical part is passed but the other parts are not, the examining board may exempt the student from repeating the practical part.
